learning_goal: Describe the clavicle's two curves, its two joints and its muscle attachments, and explain why it breaks at the junction of the curves and how the two fragments then displace.

structures.name: right clavicle
structures.label: Clavicle
structures.narration: The only bone that joins the arm to the trunk. It lies just under the skin along its whole length, so you can feel every inch of it from the notch at the front of the neck out to the point of the shoulder. Look at it from above and it is an S: the inner two-thirds curve forward, the outer third curves back.

structures.name: manubrium
structures.label: Manubrium — sternoclavicular joint
structures.narration: The medial end sits on the manubrium at the sternoclavicular joint. This is a saddle-shaped synovial joint with a complete articular disc, and it is the only synovial joint between the upper limb and the axial skeleton. The disc is why the joint almost never dislocates — force travelling down the bone breaks the shaft instead.

structures.name: right scapula
structures.label: Scapula
structures.narration: The shoulder blade. Two of its parts matter to the clavicle: the acromion it joints with, and the coracoid the holding ligament runs up from.

structures.label: Acromion
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the scapula and the clavicle — the acromioclavicular joint (gap 0.99 mm)
structures.narration: The lateral end meets the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint, a small plane synovial joint that gives very little movement. The real holding is done below it, by the coracoclavicular ligament running from the coracoid process up to the conoid tubercle and trapezoid line on the underside of the clavicle. Tear that ligament and the shoulder drops away from the bone — the step you see in a grade three separation.
structures.reviewed_note: opened in the 3D viewer and looked at: the patch lands on the feature the label names. Checked by Claude on 2026-08-28 at Frank’s request, not by an independent human reader — the measurement and its evidence are in calibrated_by.

structures.label: Coracoid process
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the point on the scapula where pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps all make contact (gaps 0.20, 0.16 and 0.14 mm; the three agree to within 12.8 mm on a 158 mm bone)
structures.narration: The hook of bone the coracoclavicular ligament runs up from to the underside of the clavicle. That ligament, not the joint above it, is what holds the shoulder up.
structures.reviewed_note: opened in the 3D viewer and looked at: the patch lands on the feature the label names. Checked by Claude on 2026-08-28 at Frank’s request, not by an independent human reader — the measurement and its evidence are in calibrated_by.

structures.label: Sternal (medial) facet
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the CONTACT PATCH between the clavicle and the manubrium, averaged over every clavicular vertex within 4 mm of the manubrium (gap 0.12 mm, 113 vertices in the patch, centroid 2.27 mm from the single nearest vertex) — the sternoclavicular articular surface
structures.narration: The saddle-shaped articular surface at the medial end. It is bigger than the shallow socket on the manubrium it sits in, which is the geometric reason the joint depends on its disc and its ligaments rather than on bony fit.

structures.label: Acromial (lateral) facet
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the CONTACT PATCH between the clavicle and the scapula, averaged over every clavicular vertex within 4 mm of the scapula (gap 0.99 mm, 65 vertices, centroid 1.32 mm from the nearest single vertex) — the clavicular half of the acromioclavicular joint. Cross-checks against the `acromion` anchor, which is the same contact measured on the scapula.
structures.narration: A small flat oval facing outward and slightly downward. Flat surfaces resist shear badly, which is why this joint separates where the medial one does not.

structures.label: Subclavian groove
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the CONTACT PATCH between the clavicle and subclavius, averaged over every clavicular vertex within 6 mm of the muscle (gap 0.22 mm, 188 vertices, centroid 1.38 mm from the nearest single vertex). A groove is a surface, not a point, so the area form was used deliberately; the patch sits at u=0.52, the middle third, which is where the groove is described.
structures.narration: The groove on the undersurface of the middle third that subclavius inserts into. It is the only muscle mark on this bone with a name of its own, and it marks the middle third — the part that breaks.

structures.name: right first rib
structures.label: 1st rib
structures.narration: The costoclavicular ligament ties the medial end of the clavicle down to the first rib and its cartilage. It is the fulcrum of the bone: every movement of the clavicle turns about it. The gap between the clavicle above and this rib below is the costoclavicular space, and the subclavian vessels and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus have to pass through it.

structures.name: right subclavius
structures.label: Subclavius
structures.narration: A small muscle running from the first costal cartilage out to the subclavian groove on the undersurface of the middle third. Its job is protective. It lies as a cushion between the bone and the vessels behind it, which is why the subclavian vessels usually survive a fractured clavicle.

structures.name: right scalenus anterior
structures.label: Scalenus anterior — the divider
structures.narration: Descends from the cervical transverse processes to the scalene tubercle of the first rib, and it is the answer to the question examiners actually ask: the vein passes in FRONT of it, the artery and the trunks of the plexus BEHIND it. Subclavius lies higher again, between all of that and the clavicle. The phrenic nerve rides down its front surface.

structures.name: right sternocleidomastoid
structures.label: Sternocleidomastoid
structures.narration: Its clavicular head takes the upper surface of the medial third. Remember this muscle when you look at a fracture film: it is what pulls the medial fragment upward.

structures.name: descending part of right trapezius
structures.label: Trapezius — descending part
structures.narration: The upper fibres of trapezius come down onto the posterior border of the lateral third. Trapezius above and deltoid below share that outer third between them, one on each border.

structures.name: clavicular part of right deltoid
structures.label: Deltoid — clavicular part
structures.narration: Deltoid takes the anterior border of the lateral third. Its front edge meets the edge of pectoralis major here, and the gap between them is the deltopectoral groove where the cephalic vein runs up to disappear under the clavicle.

structures.name: right sternohyoid
structures.label: Sternohyoid — the sixth attachment
structures.narration: A strap muscle of the neck taking a small slip from the back of the medial end of the clavicle, alongside its origin from the upper posterior manubrium and the posterior sternoclavicular ligament. Six muscles attach to this bone; this is the one most often left out of the list, because it sits behind sternocleidomastoid rather than on a surface of its own.

structures.name: clavicular part of right pectoralis major
structures.label: Pectoralis major — clavicular head
structures.narration: The clavicular head of pectoralis major arises from the front of the medial half. It is the head that flexes the arm forward, and it is the one you isolate when you press the hands together in front of the chest.

structures.name: right subclavian artery
structures.label: Subclavian artery
structures.narration: The artery crosses over the first rib behind the bone, hidden by subclavius. At the outer border of that rib it becomes the axillary artery.

structures.name: right subclavian vein
structures.label: Subclavian vein
structures.narration: The vein lies in front of the artery and slightly lower, separated from it by scalenus anterior, which descends between the two to insert on the scalene tubercle of the first rib. Subclavius lies higher again, between both vessels and the bone. A subclavian central line is aimed just under the middle of the clavicle and walked along the back of the bone precisely because the bone is the landmark you can feel and the vein is the tube you cannot.

structures.name: right internal jugular vein
structures.label: Internal jugular vein
structures.narration: The vein that comes down the neck inside the carotid sheath. Behind the sternoclavicular joint it meets the subclavian vein at the venous angle to form the brachiocephalic vein. That corner is where the lymphatic ducts empty — thoracic duct on the left, right lymphatic duct on the right — so the whole lymph of the body rejoins the blood at a junction you can point to.

structures.name: right brachiocephalic vein
structures.label: Brachiocephalic vein
structures.narration: Behind the sternoclavicular joint the subclavian vein meets the internal jugular to form the brachiocephalic vein. That corner is the venous angle, and it is where the great lymph ducts empty — the thoracic duct on the left, the right lymphatic duct on this side.

structures.name: upper lobe of right lung
structures.label: Apex of lung
structures.narration: The apex of the lung and its covering of cervical pleura rise above the first rib, behind the medial part of the clavicle. This is why a needle placed too deep under the clavicle can drop a lung, and why a pneumothorax is the complication you look for on the check film after a central line.

structures.name: right humerus
structures.label: Humerus
structures.narration: The whole weight of the arm hangs from the scapula, and the scapula hangs from the clavicle. Take the clavicle away and the shoulder falls forward and inward toward the midline.

structures.name: body of sternum
structures.label: Body of sternum
structures.narration: Below the manubrium, for orientation. The ridge where the two meet is the sternal angle, the landmark for the second costal cartilage.

views.title: The strut you can feel
views.narration: Run a finger from the notch at the base of your neck outward and you are on the clavicle the whole way. It sits horizontally across the top of the chest, subcutaneous from end to end. That is the first thing to know about it: it is the most commonly broken long bone in the body partly because there is nothing over it, and every part of it can be examined by touch.

views.title: An S seen only from above
views.narration: From the front the clavicle looks like a straight rod. From above it is clearly an S. The medial two-thirds are convex forward and roughly round in cross-section. The lateral third is concave forward and flattened from above downward. The junction of the two curves is the weakest point of the bone, and it is where the bone breaks. Learn the shape and the fracture site comes for free.

views.title: A joint at each end
views.narration: Medially it meets the manubrium at the sternoclavicular joint. Laterally it meets the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint. Both are synovial, and the medial one is the only synovial link the whole upper limb has with the axial skeleton. Compare the two facets lit here: the medial one is a saddle, deep and disc-backed, and dislocates very rarely; the lateral one is a small flat oval, weak against shear, and it separates easily — a fall on the point of the shoulder gives you the step deformity of a separated shoulder, while a fall on the outstretched hand travels up the arm and breaks the shaft.

views.title: Six muscles on one bone
views.narration: Six muscles, and dividing the bone in half sorts them out. On the medial two-thirds, four: sternocleidomastoid on the upper surface, pectoralis major on the front, subclavius underneath in its groove, sternohyoid on a small area on the back of the undersurface. On the lateral third, two: trapezius on the posterior border, deltoid on the anterior border. Count them the same way every time — four medial, two lateral, six in all. The ligaments are separate and are not in the count: the sternoclavicular capsule and the costoclavicular ligament hold the medial end down, the coracoclavicular ligament holds the lateral end up. Of the six, the two that matter for a fracture are sternocleidomastoid pulling the medial fragment up and deltoid pulling the lateral fragment down.

views.title: What is hiding behind it

ops.kind: the vein runs directly behind the middle third

views.narration: Behind the middle third, in the space between the clavicle and the first rib, lie the subclavian vein in front, the subclavian artery behind it, and the trunks of the brachial plexus behind that. Higher and further back sits the apex of the lung under its cervical pleura. Subclavius lies between all of this and the bone, which is why these structures usually escape a fracture. When they do not escape, the vein is the one most often torn, and a badly displaced medial fragment is what does it. This same anatomy is why a narrowed costoclavicular space causes thoracic outlet symptoms and why an infraclavicular central line risks a pneumothorax.

views.title: Cut through the costoclavicular space
views.narration: Cut across just under the collarbone and read from front to back. Skin and platysma, then the clavicle, then subclavius in its groove, then the subclavian vein, then the artery, then the plexus, then the first rib and the pleural dome below and behind. The clavicle above and the first rib below are the two walls of a corridor, and everything going to the arm has to travel through it. Depress the shoulder or add a cervical rib and that corridor narrows — that is the mechanism of costoclavicular thoracic outlet syndrome.

views.title: How it breaks and where the pieces go

ops.kind: opposing pulls on the two fragments

views.narration: The usual story is a fall on the outstretched hand or on the point of the shoulder. Force runs up the limb and the bone fails at the junction of its two curves, in the middle third — about eight fractures in ten sit here. Then the muscles take over. Sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial fragment up. The weight of the arm and the pull of deltoid and pectoralis major drag the lateral fragment down and forward, and pectoralis minor and the other adductors pull it medially so the two ends overlap and the shoulder shortens. The patient sits with the head tilted toward the injured side to slacken sternocleidomastoid, and supports the elbow with the other hand. Most of these unite with a sling alone, and the lump of callus you can feel afterwards is a normal finding.

views.title: First to start, last to finish
views.narration: The clavicle is the first bone in the body to begin ossifying, in the fifth week, and it is the last to finish. Most of it ossifies in membrane rather than in cartilage, which is unusual for a long bone. The epiphysis at the medial end appears late, around eighteen, and fuses around twenty-five — the last epiphysis in the skeleton to close, which makes it useful for estimating age. Two clinical consequences follow. A clavicle can break during a difficult delivery and still heal without treatment. And in cleidocranial dysostosis, where membranous ossification fails, the clavicles are absent or tiny and the patient can bring the shoulders together in front of the chest.

gaps: CORRECTED 2026-08-29 (audit). The previous note here said the clavicle mesh was not in the local set and that no surface landmark could therefore be measured. That was false: FMA13322 is on disk, and three of the five landmarks were derived at audit with tools/derive-landmark.mjs — sternal facet (contact with the manubrium, 0.12 mm, 113-vertex patch), acromial facet (contact with the scapula, 0.99 mm, 65-vertex patch, cross-checking against the `acromion` anchor which is the same joint measured from the scapula side), and subclavian groove (contact with subclavius, 0.22 mm, 188-vertex patch, all three using the --area form because a facet and a groove are surfaces and not points). All three are status needs-review: measurement proves the coordinate, only looking proves it landed on the feature.

The conoid tubercle and the trapezoid line are still narration only, and this is a definition problem rather than a delivery one. Both are defined by the coracoclavicular ligament, which has no mesh, and the scapula is not a usable substitute witness: the nearest scapular contact to the clavicle is the acromioclavicular joint, so --contact FMA13395 returns the acromial facet (uvw [0.0328,0.894,0.6573], 0.99 mm — the same point as the acromial facet anchor) and not the tubercle at all. It is a measured, reproducible and completely wrong answer, which is exactly the kind that gets believed. Recorded here so no later run re-derives it and trusts it. They become measurable the day a coracoclavicular ligament mesh exists.

None of this bone's ligaments exist as models. Re-searched at audit 2026-08-29 under ligament, ligamentum, coracoclav, costoclav, conoid, trapezoid, capsule, disc and disk: the whole catalog holds exactly four ligaments (both inguinal, both long plantar) and none is here, and the only 'capsule' hits are the internal capsule of the brain. One trap to record — FMA23725 'right trapezoid' IS in the catalog and is the CARPAL BONE, not the trapezoid line of the clavicle; do not wire it into this scene. So the costoclavicular ligament, the coracoclavicular ligament with its conoid and trapezoid parts, and the articular disc of the sternoclavicular joint — the three things that actually explain this bone's stability — are all narration. Bone-to-bone relationships stand in: the first rib for the costoclavicular ligament, the scapula for the coracoclavicular.

Platysma is named in beat 6 as the first layer of the front-to-back read and is not drawn. It is NOT absent from the catalog — FMA45739 right platysma exists — but it is not in meshes-lite/, so it could not be added without putting a model in the scene that no adapter can deliver. This is a fetch, not an authoring job, and it is the one mesh that would complete beat 6's layer sequence. 'platysma' is carried in match.terms so the beat is searchable on a structure it only describes.
No brachial plexus. Beats 5 and 6 place the trunks behind the artery in narration; the catalog holds two optic nerves and no other named nerve.
No pleura. The cervical pleura over the lung apex is the structure at risk in an infraclavicular line, and the upper lobe of the lung stands in for it.

The axillary artery and axillary vein do not exist as models, so the subclavian vessels are shown and the name change at the outer border of the first rib is narrated rather than seen. Same limitation as the pectoralis minor scene.

The joints themselves are drawn only as two bones meeting. There is no capsule, no joint space and no disc, so the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints are shown as approximations of contact rather than as articulations.
